# Pushing Water Uphill: How a City Keeps the Tap Running on the Twentieth Floor

There's a quiet miracle in the fact that you can turn a faucet on the twentieth floor of an apartment building and water comes out — reliably, at a useful pressure, at three in the morning or during the dinner rush. The system that makes this happen is a carefully engineered balance of gravity, pumps, and storage, and the best way to understand it is to follow the water through a concrete example. So imagine a mid-sized city we'll call Riverton, with a surface reservoir in the hills, a treatment plant in the valley, and a twenty-story apartment building — call it Harborview Towers — sitting on ground about 100 feet above sea level.

Start with the physics. Water is heavy — about 62.4 pounds per cubic foot — and a column of water standing in a pipe exerts pressure at its bottom purely by virtue of its height. Every foot of elevation adds roughly 0.433 psi. Engineers call this "elevation head," and it's the single most important number in water system design. If you want 40 psi at a faucet, you need the water's source surface to sit about 92 feet above that faucet. This is why water systems are organized into *pressure zones*: neighborhoods at similar elevations are grouped together and fed from sources at appropriate heights, because a single system serving both a valley and a hilltop would either drown the valley in 150 psi or leave the hilltop with a trickle.

Riverton's raw water sits in an open reservoir at elevation 150 feet. Gravity alone would carry it downhill to the treatment plant, but it can't go back up to the customers on its own. So after filtration and disinfection, the plant's high-service pump station takes over. These are big, industrial pumps — often several running in parallel with others on standby — and their job is to lift the treated water another 230 feet,
